claims.text: Urbanisation is the growth in the proportion of a country's population living in urban areas; it is a rising share of the whole population, rather than the growth of one city on its own, and Namibia's census counted about 49.5 per cent of its people in urban areas in 2023, against roughly a third at independence in 1990.

claims.text: Rapid urban growth has two engines: rural-urban migration, driven by pushes such as failing farm incomes, drought years and schooling that ends early, and by pulls such as jobs in factories and offices, secondary school places, hospital care and piped water; and natural increase, because arrivals are mostly young adults, so cities hold many births and few elderly deaths, which means the population keeps climbing even in a year when few newcomers arrive.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Saying a city offers a better standard of living, more facilities or more development explains nothing on its own, because a reader cannot picture exactly what is better; the specific pulls are more jobs in factories and offices, secondary school places, hospital care and piped water, and naming them is what turns a vague answer into a reasoned one.

claims.text: A rural area is countryside, with farmland and small settlements; the term describes the land and its settlement, and being less developed is not part of the definition.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Urban growth changes the city: arrivals build squatter settlements of self-built houses on land they do not own, where homes rise faster than services; traffic congestion follows more trips on the same streets; and water, sewerage and electricity supplies fall short, because the pipes were sized for fewer people.

claims.text: Urban growth changes the countryside people leave: fewer young adults remain, so the population structure ages and farm labour grows scarce, while the money migrants send home, remittances, supports the families that stayed.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: The answers work at both ends of the move: in the city, upgrading informal settlements in place and servicing new land with water, drains and power before settlement arrives, which reaches more households for the same budget than clearing and rebuilding; and in the countryside, developing rural roads, clinics and secondary schools so that staying is a real choice, which slows the migration that outgrows the services.

claims.text: Lagos, in Nigeria, is one of the largest cities in Africa, with an estimated 16.5 million people in 2024 and growth of hundreds of thousands a year; it was Nigeria's capital until 1991 and remains its chief port and commercial city, which is why migrants keep arriving from the rural north and east of Nigeria and from neighbouring countries.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Lagos's growth shows in named places: Makoko, the settlement of houses on stilts above the lagoon, holds thousands of families without secure land or piped water; the Bus Rapid Transit system launched in 2008 carries commuters in dedicated lanes to ease the city's traffic; and Eko Atlantic, a new district on land reclaimed from the sea behind a long sea wall, adds office and apartment ground the old city lacks.
